subject: Business
title: Positions vs. Interests
description: A 60-second lesson on Positions vs. Interests.

hook.text: Two departments demand the same conference room. That's a position. Why they need it is the interest.

buildup.text: Positions are what people say they want. Interests are why they want it.

discovery.text: Getting Past No, by William Ury, says: go behind positions to find the underlying need.

twist.text: Conflicting positions often hide compatible interests. Both departments might just need quiet space.

climax.text: Ask 'Why is that important to you?' five different ways until the real interest surfaces.

punchline.text: Fight positions and you deadlock. Explore interests and you create options.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a position and an interest?
options: A position is what someone demands; an interest is why they want it
A position is negotiable; an interest is not
Positions are emotional; interests are logical

details.summary: Positions are the specific demands people state in a negotiation, while interests are the underlying needs, fears, and desires that motivate those positions.
details.whyItMatters: Positional bargaining creates win-lose dynamics where any concession feels like a loss. Interest-based negotiation opens possibilities because different underlying needs can often be satisfied in ways that neither side initially imagined, creating
takeaways: Positions are what people demand; interests are why they demand it
Identical positions can stem from completely different underlying interests
Asking why someone wants something reveals solutions beyond their stated demands

faq.question: What is the classic example of positions versus interests?
faq.answer: Two siblings fight over the last orange, each demanding the whole thing. A position-based solution splits it in half. But one wants the juice for drinking and the other wants the peel for baking. Understanding interests gives each sibling 100 percent of what they actually need.

faq.question: How do you uncover interests when the other side only states positions?
faq.answer: Ask why they want what they are asking for. Ask what problem their position is solving. Ask what would happen if they did not get it. Listen for fears and needs beneath the stated demands. Share your own interests to model the behavior and encourage reciprocal disclosure.
